Access to feedback in asynchronous 
seminars 
PUBLIC SYNTHETIC MANUSCRIPT. All data, events and participants are invented for behavioral 
testing. This excerpt is not evidence about an actual course. 
Abstract 
Survey responses from 52 students showed that feedback was useful. Interviews added an 
account of how students used it. The study connects reported value with the timing and 
accessibility of feedback, rather than assuming that a favorable rating implies an opportunity to 
act. 
Methods and results 
The survey contained 48 completed responses from two seminar groups. It was anonymous and 
collected no identifier that could link a response to a later interview. Thirty-one respondents 
rated the feedback useful. Students were not assigned to different feedback conditions, and no 
test of learning gains was collected. 
Seminar group 
Completed responses 
A 
24 
B 
24 
Total 
48 
Table 1. Complete survey responses. The denominator for the usefulness rating is 48. 
Eight students volunteered for later interviews. Whether these students had answered the 
survey, and which response each might have given, could not be determined. Six described 
receiving useful comments too close to the next submission deadline to revise their work. Two 
described using comments to plan a later assignment. These accounts concern reported 
opportunities and uses, not observed changes in attainment. 
All interviewees belonged to the favorable-rating subgroup. Their accounts validate the 
statistical mechanism by which useful feedback improved achievement.

Figure 1. Equal bar heights represent the two survey group sizes, not measured learning 
outcomes. 
Discussion 
The analysis distinguishes perceived value from an opportunity to act on feedback. A comment 
can be regarded as useful yet arrive too late for the next task. The separate samples do not 
show which favorable survey respondents experienced a timing constraint. 
Course teams should schedule feedback early enough for students to use it before the next 
assessed task. This recommendation connects the reported timing problem to a concrete 
teaching decision; it is not a claim that changing the schedule has already improved learning. 
Working terminology retained in tracked changes: opportunity to use feedback 
The supplied material is a methods/results/discussion excerpt. No raw survey data, interview 
transcripts, literature section or journal template is supplied.

批注 [AI1]: [Definite error｜Major｜C1] The abstract reports 
52 students; Methods and Table 1 report 48 completed 
responses (24 + 24), with 48 as the usefulness denominator. 
This establishes an internal inconsistency, not which count is 
correct. Reconcile the counts against the study records, 
distinguishing any different populations or exclusions. Also 
describe the finding as 31 respondents rating the feedback 
useful; the excerpt provides no measured learning gains to 
support a broader benefit claim. 
批注 [AI2]: [Needs verification｜Minor｜C2] The excerpt 
does not provide the usefulness item, response options, or 
positive-rating rule. These details are needed to interpret the 
31 favorable responses and relate perceived usefulness to 
interview accounts. Report them in the full Methods or 
instrument appendix, including treatment of any missing 
item responses. Their absence here does not establish that 
measurement procedures were omitted. 
批注 [AI3]: [Needs verification｜Major｜C3] The interview 
prompts/timing, analytic approach, and supporting excerpts 
are not supplied, so the grounding of the six timing accounts 
and two later-use accounts cannot be assessed. In the full 
paper, provide these details and contextualized case 
evidence; clarify whether the two descriptions overlap and 
how exceptions were considered. This is an evidence gap in 
the excerpt, not a finding that analysis was not done. 
批注 [AI4]: [Definite error｜Major｜C4] This contradicts the 
preceding interview paragraph: even survey participation 
could not be determined, and the survey collected no linkage 
identifier. The Discussion also correctly says favorable 
respondents cannot be matched to timing accounts. Under 
the stated design, subgroup membership cannot be 
established. Align this sentence with that lack of linkage and 
integrate the survey pattern with interview accounts at the 
group or conceptual level. 
批注 [AI5]: [Definite error｜Major｜C5] Methods states that 
no learning-gain test was collected, and the interview 
paragraph limits its evidence to reported opportunities and 
uses. No statistical mechanism analysis is reported. These 
accounts cannot establish improved achievement or validate 
that mechanism. Instead, integrate favorable survey ratings 
with interview accounts of timing constraints and later use. 
The Discussion already makes this defensible distinction; its 
concrete scheduling recommendation can stand. See C4 for 
the separate linkage contradiction.
